summary: Kitsap County summit: wooden lookout towers from 1928, an 84-ft L-4 tower in 1942, last tower (1963) gone by 1971; a microwave tower stood there in 2014.

facts.design: 84-foot treated timber tower with L-4 cab (1942)
facts.status_note: Last lookout tower (1963, 50 ft) removed or destroyed in 1971; a single microwave tower on the summit as of 2014; no source describes remains of the lookout

access.note: In Green Mountain State Forest; a forest road open to motorized traffic reaches the summit and established trails climb it

visit.trail_note: Established trails climb to the summit; a forest road open to motorized traffic reaches the summit picnic area

resolved_conflicts.explanation: FFLOS dates the first 50-foot tower to 1928. The Washington Forest Fire Association report quoted by WashingtonLookouts dates it to 1929, and WillhiteWeb calls 1929 the first known structure. The story gives both years.

WashingtonLookouts and WillhiteWeb put the reconstruction to 97 feet in 1931. FFLOS says a 90-foot wooden tower replaced the first tower in 1933. The story reports the 1931 rebuild and mentions the register's 1933 date.
Air Warning Service activation is March 15, 1942 per WashingtonLookouts and March 15, 1943 per WillhiteWeb. Both give October 16, 1943 as the deactivation date.
FFLOS blames vandals who released the guy wires. WashingtonLookouts says vandals destroyed the tower. WillhiteWeb says a scout troop took the guy lines, thinking the lookout was no longer in use.
FFLOS says the 1963 tower was destroyed in 1971. WillhiteWeb says it was removed or destroyed. The story uses the register's wording with WillhiteWeb's caveat.

notes_for_editor: Brief design L-4 is right for the 1942 tower. height_m is 25.6 (the 84-ft timber tower, per FFLOS); the earlier 15.2 value was the 50-ft wooden tower and has been corrected. Many dates conflict across sources (1928/1929, 1931/1933, AWS 1942/1943, 1962 cause, 1971 fate); all are reported in the story. Staffing names come only from WillhiteWeb, a hobby site; they are sourced but single-sourced. Access: the Wikipedia forest-road claim is the only access source; no DNR page was read. Brief's 2012 FFLOS registration verified.
